scores.evidence: hosted fields or Checkout keep us at PCI SAQ A (reduced scope, not zero)
scores.rationale: Claims about Stripe event retention, SAQ A scope, RLS fail-closed behavior, ledger write-rate math and idempotency semantics are all accurate, including the subtle areas where billing plans usually err.

scores.evidence: It covers the plan catalog, subscriptions, metered usage, rating, invoicing, payments, tax, dunning, reconciliation
scores.rationale: Covers nearly all implied core billing needs with explicit, justified deferrals, but trials/pauses, billing anchors/time zones, and a dunning retry schedule are left undefined.

scores.evidence: Ledger favors consistency: a single primary, serializable posting, append-only, corrections by credit note only
scores.rationale: Consistency, tenancy, idempotency and async choices are made once and honored everywhere (phases, validations, cross-cutting table) with no internal contradictions.

scores.evidence: kill workers mid-posting, replay each webhook 3×, reorder webhooks, run two bill-run workers on one tenant-period
scores.rationale: V0–V9 tie checkable thresholds to the specific money, isolation and metering risks, validate the riskiest decisions (V1, V3, V4) before commitment, and continue in production via daily reconciliation.

scores.evidence: fee basis ASSUMPTION: about 0.5–0.8% of billed revenue
scores.rationale: Every figure is labeled ASSUMPTION or UNKNOWN with a named supplier and deadline, and the ranked missing-inputs list states exactly how the design changes if each assumption is wrong.

scores.evidence: No retry, duplicate, crash or concurrency sequence can double-charge, lose a payment or unbalance the ledger
scores.rationale: Covers the hard domain failures — duplicates, out-of-order webhooks, partial crashes, cross-tenant tampering, provider/tax outages, broker loss, data loss — each with concrete detection, containment and recovery.

scores.evidence: Alerts: error rate, outbox lag, webhook signature failures, consumer lag
scores.rationale: Deployment, expand-only migrations, rehearsed rollback, domain-meaningful alerts (ledger invariants, reconciliation), runbooks, DR drill and an on-call-load exit check are all sized to a stated 3–6 person team.

scores.evidence: compare 3-year vendor fees with the build-and-run estimate
scores.rationale: Vendor fees, pipeline storage cost and team-size constraints are identified with labeled bases and budget exit checks, but the build-and-run side is deferred to the V1 spike with no order-of-magnitude estimate in the plan.

scores.evidence: Then buy the engine, keep our own metering, and demote our ledger to a reconciliation mirror
scores.rationale: Every decision carries an R2/R3 reversibility class, revisit trigger and explicit exit path (schema-per-tenant flip, home_region seam, per-tenant fallback to manual), with the only true point of no return gated by V9.

scores.evidence: One billing service, one managed Postgres, one managed stream, object storage... No self-hosted clusters
scores.rationale: A modular monolith with managed services, a long justified deferral list, and each component earning its place; the one heavier element (Kafka/raw store) is justified by replay/re-rating and kept replaceable.

scores.evidence: Run the §4 request end to end; deploy and roll back through the pipeline; break the webhook endpoint
scores.rationale: A concrete $1 end-to-end first slice, dependency-justified phase order, per-phase exit checks, and an explicit 'if it fails' path for every validation let a team start immediately.
